Business.title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
Business.text:
The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt.

Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night.

This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers.

Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after.

Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working.

Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership.

But how much of this was due to nationalisation?

The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems.

But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents.

Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages.

TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations.

A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do.

So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August.

It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over.

Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff.

But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England.

"The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers."

Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats.

But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations - can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working?

"I think it's completely hopeless to try and do that assessment over such a short period," Stephen Glaister, a former chair of regulator the Office of Rail and Road who is now emeritus professor of transport and infrastructure at Imperial College London. He thinks a decade is needed to assess the impact of nationalisation.

The government argues that official data suggests publicly owned train operators are performing better on punctuality and cancellations overall than those still under DfT contracts to private operators.

Experts point out that whoever is running the passenger trains, some limitations remain. Many delays happen because infrastructure, like signals, fails. There's only so much capacity on the existing network. And getting better trains or more staff can take years.

The view that privatisation ultimately failed, leaving unreliable services and high fares, may be widespread. However, Prof Glaister argues that for a few years in the 1990s, the old privatised system actually worked well. Operating costs and subsidies were falling while the number of train services and passengers went up, he says.

And in the current context, it's important to be clear about what nationalisation really means.

The railways Labour inherited weren't, in truth, completely privatised, and nationalisation doesn't mean a return to British Rail.

For example, the infrastructure manager Network Rail has been fully under public control for over two decades. A number of train companies including LNER and Northern had already been nationalised under the Conservatives. Scotrail, Transport for Wales and Caledonian Sleeper are controlled by devolved national governments.

And even those operators still on contracts issued by the DfT at Westminster have been heavily controlled by the government for years. During Covid, private operators started being paid a fixed fee to run services, while the taxpayer took on the financial risk. The terms of the contracts meant train companies had to "ask government for permission to blow their nose", according to one senior industry executive, who asked not to be named so they could speak freely.

Highly profitable rolling stock companies ("ROSCOS") still own the actual trains. Freight companies operate privately too, and there are a handful of fully commercial "open access operators" on the rails like Lumo, Hull Trains and Grand Central - although there are concerns within the industry that these could end up squeezed.

So what is often referred to as the nationalisation of the railways, in fact amounts to gradually returning passenger train operators run by private companies to public hands as their contracts expire - and making this the default.

This is not all that's happening, though. The government hopes that re-organising the railways under a new publicly run body, Great British Railways (GBR), will make a big difference. This will bring together the running of trains and tracks, ending the current fragmented system.

A botched rail timetable introduction in 2018 was the spark for the then-Conservative government to eventually propose GBR as a new overarching body - although the Tories believe private competition should not be excluded from the system.

Some trains are already covered in distinctive GBR branding, but the organisation still doesn't exist. A new law to create it is making its way through parliament. Unknowns remain, like exactly how GBR will interact with devolved governments, and who its senior leaders will be.

Transport expert and author Prof Jon Shaw, of the University of Plymouth, says the idea of a "single guiding mind" should create "a better planned railway that's more aligned to the customer".

Prof Shaw thinks potential benefits include better long-term planning around rolling-stock and timetables, and the removal of "the compensation merry-go-round", where train companies and Network Rail argue about whose fault a delay was.

Hynes says: "The way you get the railway to work is you get the infrastructure and the trains and the people working in harmony because it's a system. And we can do that in a publicly owned GBR railway in a way that we haven't been able to do for a generation."

But Prof Shaw cautions of potential pitfalls. For example, "there remains very little money", and "a massive issue is whether or not the rail minister or DfT more generally - or the Treasury - will be able to butt out" and leave rail leaders to run the railway.

Prof Glaister also fears politically sensitive aspects such as fares and levels of service could lead to politicians trying to run the railways themselves, because of the amount of public money involved.

"Actually, governments are not very good at running railways," he says. "So you want management who are somewhat independent and able to run it."

Lord Hendy insists that despite the Transport Secretary having ultimate sign-off on GBR's strategy, the body will be genuinely arms-length from government.

"The point of this is to get a cadre of people who are committed to the outcomes that the secretary of state and I want for it, who can go off and run it on their own," he says, adding: "They'll have a lot more chance in the future than they've had in the last 20 years."

The railways are currently subsidised to the tune of around £12bn a year - not including spending on major projects like HS2.

The Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander says that she wants to see subsidy levels fall. Meanwhile, Network Rail has acknowledged a squeezed budget means difficult choices, and shoring up the network against the effects of more extreme weather requires investment.

Prof Glaister says: "When the public is hoping for a better level of service, more reliability, fewer breakdowns and lower fares, what they're really asking for is more money to be put into the railway.

"I don't think it's likely the government is going to be able to find more money, probably [it will have] less, actually. And so I think there's a real problem with ministers raising expectations from this policy."

But Hynes doesn't see a contradiction between reducing taxpayer subsidy and making train services better.

"My two north stars are performance up and subsidy down," he says. "If the service is better, we get more customers, we get more revenue."

Lord Hendy and Hynes also push back on the idea that the answer to improving reliability might be running fewer trains.

Hynes says: "In an industry with high fixed costs, the best way of getting the subsidy down is to go for growth."

Questions also remain about how GBR will manage industrial relations. Terms and conditions currently vary across operators. What will cost-conscious ministers do if unions seek to standardise these at the most generous level across the network?

While ministers argue they are getting on with improvements that people will notice, there's acknowledgement that the speed of improvement will vary between operators.

Lord Hendy says some changes "ought to be dead boring… to make sure tomorrow is a little better than today if you can do it".

But he says "more than 30 years worth of behaviors" will need altering to make the railway run solely in the interests of the customer.

At Woking, is there optimism that things will improve in the long run?

"I really hope so," says Leo, "it would be amazing - as it's not the best service now."

Business.title: How to avoid getting stung with bad debt advice if you miss a credit card payment
Business.text:
An increasing number of people are missing credit card repayments as finances are stretched by rising bills, according to the Bank of England.

Lenders also told the Bank they expected the number of unpaid credit card debts to keep going up this autumn.

This could lead to more demand for advice on how to deal with debts – but, if you are struggling and need help, there are some traps to avoid.

And it is worth remembering that impartial advice is available free of charge from debt charities. So here's what to think about.

If you find yourself with money troubles, it can be tempting to seize any opportunity to get things back on track.

Social media and internet search pages are full of supposed quick-fix debt solutions. Cold calls and WhatsApp messages also promise debt help.

But they may well come with upfront fees, unrealistic claims about writing off debt, and pressure to make a quick decision.

Suggestions on the best way to find help include:

Impartial, authorised debt advice comes free. You can find a provider on the government-backed Moneyhelper website, external

Check whether a firm offering debt help is authorised by the regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). You should cross-check the authorisation details they give with the FCA's Firm Checker, external

Anyone unhappy with the service from an authorised firm can complain and, if you are still not happy, go to the independent Financial Ombudsman Service.

Alison Walters, director of consumer finance at the FCA, said: "Anyone struggling with debt deserves advice that puts their interests first.

"Free, impartial debt advice is available to everyone, and no one should be pressured or misled into paying for a debt solution that may not be right for them."

Business.title: Healey faces £35bn Budget challenge to meet spending pledges, says think tank
Business.text:
Chancellor John Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that if the government wants to raise defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030 and lift health spending without squeezing other departments, it will need a "top-up" of billions of pounds.

Higher inflation, caused by the Iran war, could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the IFS said.

The Treasury declined to comment.

The government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.

The IFS said that Healey must set out "credible" spending plans in the Budget, which will take place on 28 October.

"A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller.

"Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course.

"Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.

Speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home.

"But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together."

He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".

Miller told the BBC's Today programme that Healey had inherited spending plans for government departments where spending growth would slow in the coming years.

"[It] already looked likely that he would have to make spending cuts just to live within those," she said. "Now, along comes the Middle East war, inflation goes up and those spending plans look very tight indeed."

Added to that, the chancellor has said he wants to get defence spending up to 3% of national income. Under Keir Starmer's leadership, Healey resigned as defence secretary in June in a battle with the Treasury over military spending.

Miller said: "You put all that together, if he wanted to do all of that within current spending plans he's looking at having to cut some other services by something like £35bn."

She said the government would have a "tough time" if it wanted to raise taxes to stop cuts to departments and fund defence spending.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced billions of pounds in tax rises. Meanwhile, Labour pledged in its manifesto "not increase taxes on working people", ruling out rises to National Insurance, income tax or VAT. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will stick to that promise.

Miller said: "You'd really have to be scaping around and doing lots of small things to get up to big sums."

Business.title: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF
Business.text:
The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.

In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.

“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, and the UK and euro area potentially more insulated – though investors with US holdings would be hit.

Athanasios Vamvakidis, the deputy director of the IMF’s monetary and capital department, launching the report, said: “The exposure of the rest of the world to US assets, particularly AI, is the highest it has ever been. So this is supporting the global economy through wealth effects today; but if we get a market correction it could have broad implications.”

An AI crash was one of three “salient risks” to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack.

It called this trio of factors “plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”.

The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector.

“Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures, and circular financing arrangements,” it said.

Such a reassessment would then “sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers”.

The “magnificent seven” big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35% of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12% a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50% in the past two years.

Yet the IMF warned of “growing evidence” that the successful rollout of AI “may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by ‘hyperscaler’ firms”, and “potential economic gains may not be as large as expected”.

The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle.

Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers. Reports that the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT was making good progress on a new chip architecture also hit South Korean tech companies.

The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash.

In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves; hedge fund investment in the sector; and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks.

In the event of an AI-led market downturn “these growing sources of leverage heighten the potential for forced selling and surges in equity volatility”, it said.

It also pointed to the prevalence of “circular financing” deals, tying stronger AI companies to weaker partners in the same sector, and potentially exacerbating the impact of a share price correction.

It identified $300bn (£227bn) worth of transactions between hyperscalers and “weaker AI firms” in just the past three years, supplemented by $650bn in debt, in exchange for $1.4tn in future financial commitments.

In London, the chief executive of the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, Nikhil Rathi, urged every small business across the financial sector to take out insurance to protect themselves against AI-related cybersecurity threats.

He told MPs on the Commons Treasury committee that not all companies would have the resources to pay for access to “frontier” AI models such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which has been released on a restricted basis after it was said to be rapidly identifying gaps in government and corporate cybersecurity systems.

“One message I’d give to every small business: you should consider making sure you are insured,” Rathi said.

Business.title: Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises
Business.text:
Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.

Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000).

“New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said.

These models improved on John Maynard Keynes’s stabilisation models, which struggled to handle the impact of the oil shock in the 1970s, when countries suffered high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment at the same time.

Hall and Woodford demonstrated how traditional models could be reconstructed, based on how individual households and businesses collectively affect an economy through their actions.

Hall’s work was based on forward-looking consumer behaviour rather than the more mechanical rules of thumb used by Keynes, which linked key variables such as inflation, unemployment and gross domestic product (GDP).

Woodford built on this work to create the New Keynesian model, a full macroeconomic stabilisation framework that is the main tool for policymakers now.

This model was used after the 2008 financial crisis by policymakers as they steered the global economy away from the risk of a second great depression.

“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, the chair of the committee for the economics prize, said.

Hall and Woodford’s work also led to the development of forward guidance, where central bankers communicate where they expect interest rates to be in the future. That became an important tool after the 2008 financial crisis, and the Covid pandemic, when interest rates were cut to record lows.

Forward guidance has had its critics, though – the current chair of the US Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, has argued it should only have a “limited and circumscribed” role in normal times, to avoid “creating ambiguity in the name of clarity”.

And in 2014, the then Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, was labelled an “unreliable boyfriend” for dropping hints over interest rate rises that never came to pass.

Woodford said he was “elated”. “It’s a tremendous honour. It’s a surprise but I’m feeling very good about it,” he told reporters in Stockholm by phone after receiving the news.

The Columbia University president, Jennifer L Mnookin, said: “I offer my deepest congratulations to Michael Woodford on this tremendous honour.

“What a tribute to his groundbreaking work alongside Robert E Hall that has fundamentally reshaped the theoretical foundations of stabilisation policy and provided us with the tools to navigate economic upturns and downturns more effectively.”

Hall is also known for coining the idea that US economists can be divided into freshwater and saltwater varieties.

The fresh water group, who tend to be based at inland universities located near the Great Lakes, such as the University of Chicago, believe in free markets, neoclassical price theory, rational expectations and monetarism.

Salt water economists, though, cluster at coastal universities, such as Harvard, MIT, UC Berkeley, Yale, Princeton, UCLA and Columbia. They tend to be Keynesians and New Keynesians, believing that governments and central banks can affect demand in their economies.

The economics Nobel prize is not one of the five created by Alfred Nobel. Instead, it was invented by Sweden’s central bank, and is known as the Sveriges Riksbank prize in economic sciences in memory of Alfred Nobel.

Sports.title: Man City charges: Football regulator will quit if independence compromised
Sports.text:
The head of English football's independent regulator says he will resign if he encounters any political interference over the future of Manchester City.

As chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan has the power to assess the suitability of club owners and executives.

If an independent commission's findings that the club broke Premier League financial rules are upheld, the watchdog would have to decide whether to force a sale.

Last month, the Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owners decided to sell up.

When asked about Burnham's comments, Kogan told BBC Sport: "The Prime Minister is entirely entitled to make his own observations on anything.

"We are independent. That is in the name. I am the chairman of the Independent Football Regulator and independence absolutely runs through everything we're doing.

"And no politician has tried to influence and would try to influence anything we do on that."

When asked what he would do if he did come under political pressure over the case, Kogan replied: "I would resign."

An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations. City insist they are innocent and have appealed.

The prime minister initially told the BBC of his concerns, before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".

However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process.

Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanded all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club are released. The government released these details on Monday.

"As far as we, as the regulator, are concerned, we have a very, very clear course of action that is governed by statute and we are going to follow that course of action and no comment by any politician or indeed any individual is going to affect what we do", said Kogan.

"Process is going to drive what we do. Process will lead us to a conclusion.

"We cannot reach any conclusion at this stage because we don't know the outcome of any appeal and once we do then we will act accordingly."

Kogan's hiring as IFR chair was the subject of an inquiry by the Commissioner for Public Appointments over his historic links to the Labour Party, having contributed money to the leadership campaigns of former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer and culture secretary Lisa Nandy.

Shadow Culture Minister Louie French has written to the government, citing "concerns about the IFR's ability to adjudicate this case fairly, free from political interference".

In response, Kogan said: "I can tell you absolutely categorically that any politician who's trying to meddle in this for political purposes is welcome to try and welcome to do it, but I am going to stand by the probity of the organisation that I lead. If anybody wishes to challenge those after we've acted, that's entirely up to them."

The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing - which could take months to convene - to decide the punishment.

City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving the club and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.

City's punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or being ejected from the Premier League.

Asked how crucial it is that it was resolved as soon as possible, Kogan said: "I think it's very important."

Kogan added that the case was "raising very serious issues if Manchester City on appeal is found to be guilty of the allegations within those findings".

"We are waiting like everybody else to see what the independent panel will do… and then we will bring in a view in terms of our own investigation and statutory powers if we need to do so.

"Our powers relate to individual owners, directors and senior executives. They refer to whether people are in a position to run a club in a way that is safe, coherent and done with probity, and we will be examining those things."

An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 that led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation.

The commission's report said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".

Sports.title: African Grand Prix: Why Rwanda has been chosen to host Formula 1
Sports.text:
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.

Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.

But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.

Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.

That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.

Morocco never found the finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.

For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.

The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.

At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.

The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.

But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.

"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".

"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.

"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."

From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.

He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.

And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.

Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.

The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.

President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.

Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.

"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."

Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that the project is using money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.

Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.

The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.

But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.

The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.

Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.

F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.

Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.

F1 is not blind to such issues. Its own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders to address any issues that arise.

It also says it focuses its efforts "in relation to those areas which are within our own direct influence".

A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."

But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.

"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.

"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."

Sports.title: South Africa vs Australia: The questions posed after Proteas' heavy defeat
Sports.text:
First Test, Durban (day five of five)

Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56

South Africa 284 & 206: Markram 75; Hazlewood 6-49

Australia won by 214 runs

South Africa's 12-match unbeaten run came to a shuddering stop with defeat against Australia in Durban, but were they simply rusty or is there more to read into a Test match in which they were outclassed across the five days?

The world champions held on until an hour into the afternoon session on the final day – Aiden Markram fought admirably for 237 deliveries – but Australia, led by Josh Hazlewood with career-best figures of 6-49, eventually broke any lingering resistance to go 1-0 up in the three-match series.

"I would like to see more fight," said Proteas coach Shukri Conrad. "I don't know if it is alarming [but] it is concerning."

So should South Africa be worried at the start of an eye-catching few months which includes the visit of England over Christmas?

Much was made of South Africa's run to the 2025 World Test Championship final at Lord's.

They played only 12 Tests – no team played fewer – and qualified after drawing at home against India and losing in New Zealand, before beating West Indies, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Pakistan.

Mitigation for this latest Test also comes from the fact this is their first in almost a year and the majority of their batters played one domestic red-ball match to prepare.

Australia recently came off an eight-month break of their own and lost to Bangladesh in home conditions, as Conrad was keen to point out.

And last summer's famous win over Australia and a 2-0 success in India proves they can beat the world's top teams.

However, this Test only reinforced a worrying trend among South Africa's batters.

Tristan Stubbs and Ryan Rickelton are fine white-ball players, but Stubbs' two Test centuries have come against Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, and Rickelton's against Sri Lanka and Pakistan.

This was an obvious step up.

In the first innings, Stubbs, two overs after Wiaan Mulder had been bounced out, top-edged a pull to fine leg, and in the second he played a loose drive on one.

Opener Rickelton drove and edged at a wide ball late on day two and nicked through a pull in the fourth over on day four.

Similarly, Mulder scored 367 not out against Zimbabwe last year, but Bangladesh are the only other side he averages more than 30 against. His 110-ball stay for 29 on the final day before being strangled down the leg side was at least encouraging.

Wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, in contrast, lasted only three balls before nudging Matt Renshaw's part-time spin to slip. His Test average of 30.14 drops to 28 against Australia and 15 against both England and India.

Conrad said that "a few of the guys need to step up".

"The real disappointment was the batting in the first dig on a really good wicket," Conrad said.

"Yes, a world-class attack, but quite a few guys getting starts and not kicking on."

Aiden Markram's defiant knock in the fourth innings, in which he batted for almost six hours for 75 runs before edging Mitchell Starc through to Alex Carey in the afternoon session, was one positive for the Proteas.

David Bedingham also looked comfortable in his new position of number three, albeit he was one of those guilty of failing to make the most of starts after reaching 49 and 46.

This defeat was not solely on the batters, either.

Bavuma, who tasted defeat as captain for the first time in this match, allowed the game to drift on day two as Australia extended their score from 124-6 to 390 not out.

Australia's Matt Renshaw played brilliantly for his 190 but was not challenged as he casually farmed the strike and protected Nathan Lyon in their ninth-wicket stand of 134.

And while judging them against Australia's fearsome attack, the most successful quartet Test cricket has seen, is hardly fair, South Africa's bowlers lacked the relentless pressure of their counterparts.

Anrich Nortje was impressive in taking four wickets in his first Test since March 2023. His last spell was quicker than his first as he brought pace and hostility, hitting Steve Smith on the helmet with a bouncer on day four.

But Mulder offered little after his new-ball spells and Marco Jansen was quiet after dismissing Nic Maddinson and Steve Smith on day one.

The return from injury of their premier quick Kagiso Rabada, who was seen bowling at lunch on day five, cannot come soon enough.

Spinners Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj did not escape Conrad's gaze either.

"Anrich's return was phenomenal and really pleasing," Conrad said.

"If we were brutally honest, our spinners were not as sharp as they normally are."

With the second Test starting in only five days' time in Gqeberha, South Africa must hope this Test has removed the rust.

The alternate takeaway would be far more concerning.

Sports.title: Florian Wirtz: Should Liverpool drop Germany playmaker?
Sports.text:
At the end of the 2024-25 season, Liverpool head coach Arne Slot flew to the south of France to honour talks with Rayan Cherki.

Cherki was on Liverpool's shortlist in their hunt for an attacking midfielder but the main target was Florian Wirtz - who was also wanted by Bayern Munich and Manchester City.

Once Wirtz said his preference was to move to Anfield and join the then-Premier League champions, the £116m deal became a formality.

At the time, his arrival felt like a quality acquisition for Liverpool, but more than a year on things are still not clicking.

The German has scored seven goals and provided 11 assists over 56 Reds appearances, but had no goal involvements against any of the top-10 teams in the Premier League last season.

This term, Wirtz has started every game in the league and Champions League so far - managing just one assist across seven matches.

Those struggles were summed up on Sunday against Manchester City when new Reds boss Andoni Iraola - who succeeded Slot in the summer - replaced Wirtz with Trey Nyoni in the 66th minute, shortly after Ryan Gravenberch was sent off and Erling Haaland broke the deadlock.

Wirtz is only 23 but so is Cherki, who put the icing on the cake in City's 3-0 win at Anfield with an exquisite goal - the kind we have become used to seeing since his £30m move from Lyon in June 2025.

Cherki cost less than a third of what Liverpool paid for Wirtz, but has already scored 16 goals and provided 18 assists in 65 City appearances.

The France attacker has also shown an ability to provide crucial game-changing moments. Liverpool fans haven't seen anywhere near enough of that from Wirtz yet.

"Wirtz has so much ability. I wish I had that ability because he just glides. He makes it look effortless - but he doesn't hurt teams," former Liverpool defender Steven Warnock told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"He doesn't impact the game enough. He drifts in and out of games. He's here for 10 or 20 seconds and then he disappears for five or 10 minutes and you think where is he now?"

After Liverpool's defeat by Man City, Jamie Carragher said it was time for Iraola to drop Wirtz.

"I think he needs to come out of the team, I said that last time out and I'm going to say it again," Carragher told Sky Sports.

"Liverpool played well [against Man City] for a lot of the game before the Gravenberch red card but they didn't create a chance, so they have a real problem with scoring goals and creating chances and that's what you got Wirtz for.

"He's not giving you anything defensively and he's not giving you anything going the other way. I don't want anyone to pile in on the lad but I think we're justified in saying we need more and we can't wait."

Given that Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai are all currently sidelined, it would be a big call to drop Wirtz - but Liverpool have two games every week between now and the November international break.

With Gravenberch suspended for Saturday's trip to Brentford, Iraola will likely keep the Dutch midfielder in for Wednesday's Champions League game against LASK in Austria and give a start to Nyoni. More changes are expected from Sunday's defeat.

When it comes to the intensity of the top flight, Wirtz is still finding his feet, but his best performance this season came in the Champions League against Atletico Madrid and he was unlucky not to get an assist when Bradley Barcola fired wide.

Asked on Tuesday if Wirtz needed more time, Iraola defended his player and said: "The other day, he probably he didn't have his best game but he has had good games with us this season.

"Everyone starts looking for answers. He had some good performances in the national team - he scored one goal and he will have better or worse games.

"But I would like to look at it more collectively and more how they help us play and get results and after that I don't care who scores. I think it's a more collective thing."

Seeing Wirtz excel for Germany under Jurgen Klopp is proof - if it was needed - as to why he was seen as one of the hottest talents in world football when he joined Liverpool.

"Attacking players always need a functioning team that works well around them. Anyone who loves football can still see how outstanding Florian is as a player," Klopp said recently.

That is also a view shared by Steven Gerrard.

"I can just picture him beating himself up on how his Liverpool thing has started. This kid is a major talent in my opinion. I've seen enough to believe and give him a chance. I think he needs help and support now," Gerrard told The Overlap.

Wirtz created 95 chances from open play in all competitions last season - at least 27 more than any other Liverpool player - and his fizzing pass for Victor Munoz's equaliser against Nottingham Forest in August showed a glimpse of his class, but those moments have been few and far in between.

Against City at the weekend there was a moment at 0-0 when Wirtz hit an effort wide despite having Barcola and Milos Kerkez in space on his left. It was a poor decision from a man desperate for a big moment.

Back in August, Wirtz spoke candidly about how he felt "more ready" for his second season at Anfield. The physicality was a key aspect, with bulking up a big focus of his first campaign.

"I definitely learned a lot. I just learned how Premier League football is played and I think I am more ready for my second season because I know how it is now. I am really excited for my next season," Wirtz said then.

He impressed in pre-season but two months into the new campaign, Wirtz needs to start delivering sooner rather than later.

If not, then Iraola will be left with a tough decision to make.

Sports.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: What represents success for England & home nations?
Sports.text:
"Do I believe we can win? It's not a no. Anybody who says we can't win with a finality to it - that's not my belief."

England's new men's head coach Brian McDermott has sounded a note of hope going into the Rugby League World Cup. And he is not the only coach looking forward with optimism. For now at least, everybody harbours a dream.

Not everyone taking part in the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments over the next month is expecting to come away with a winner's medal - but they all have a target for success. For some, it's a title. For others, it's showing progress, or creating a legacy.

The men's competition kicks off first, on Thursday (10:05 BST), with reigning champions Australia facing New Zealand in a Sydney blockbuster dubbed a potential dress rehearsal for the final.

Both will certainly have their sights on lifting the trophy in Brisbane on 15 November.

It is a similar story for Australia's women - seeking a fourth successive title - as they begin their campaign against Samoa in Sydney on Friday (10:05 BST).

England, meanwhile, have high hopes of retaining their wheelchair title - they start against Wales in Wollongong on Friday, 30 October (04:30 BST).

Australia is hosting the bulk of the the three tournaments - including all of the wheelchair matches - with Papua New Guinea staging two men's and two women's games and New Zealand one of each.

Here, BBC Sport examines what would represent success at this World Cup for England, the home nations and the tournament as a whole.

Four years ago, England's men suffered a gut-wrenching 27-26 golden-point World Cup semi-final defeat by Samoa at Emirates Stadium.

Series wins over Tonga in 2023 and Samoa a year later banished some of those memories - but last autumn brought a 3-0 home series loss to Australia.

The manner of that defeat led to Shaun Wane's departure and a new head coach in McDermott, who is seeking to lead England to only their second final since 1995.

However, prior to his squad's arrival Down Under last week, the Gold Coast Titans assistant had not even had the benefit of a training session with his players.

There was no mid-season international this year to help England prepare for a World Cup programme that begins on Saturday against a powerful Tonga side packed with NRL talent.

England then take on France and Papua New Guinea in Pool B-C - a combined six-team group from which the top two will reach the semi-finals.

Yet despite limited preparation opportunities, England will have hope of reaching a fourth final if they find their rhythm.

McDermott's 23-man squad boasts arguably the best centre in the world in Dolphins star Herbie Farnworth, while lock Victor Radley has just helped Sydney Roosters win the Grand Final in Australia.

They are two of 10 NRL-based players selected by the former Leeds boss, who has taken advantage of utilising heritage players to call up versatile Roosters back Hugo Savala and Brisbane Broncos front-rower Ben Talty.

Huddersfield-born Canterbury Bulldogs prop Max King, who has previously appeared for New South Wales in State of Origin, will also make his bow, and with Harry Smith among seven Wigan players in contention, there will be no shortage of big-game experience in England's ranks.

While England showed plenty of passion and physicality against Australia in 2025, McDermott has emphasised that more guile is required in attack.

"We have got to do things differently," McDermott said.

"Being passionate to play for England is huge. You have to be aggressive to play our game, you have to be a warrior, a gladiator - but you have to have some smart attack as well.

"You have to play with a point of difference and attack into certain areas. I don't believe too many England teams have done that over the years."

England's women, ranked third in the world, travel to Australia with memories still fresh of their record 90-4 defeat by the Jillaroos in Las Vegas in March 2025.

They will meet again at this World Cup - a Group A fixture against the world champions is bookended by matches against Wales and a showdown with Samoa in Wollongong that could determine whether they reach the last four for the fifth time.

The complexion of Stuart Barrow's squad has altered dramatically - a youthful and dynamic squad features only six of the team who featured in Nevada.

It is buoyed by the inclusion of Australia-born Jasmin Strange, with the Sydney Roosters second-row forward joined by another heritage player - Hope Millard of Canterbury Bulldogs.

Barrow's squad is also enhanced by the return of Australia-based Fran Goldthorp, Georgia Roche and Hollie-Mae Dodd.

St Helens' loose forward Jodie Cunningham, 34, provides valuable experience in her fourth and final World Cup. The new headline acts include a Wigan trio - 19-year-old Woman of Steel Jenna Foubister, Megan Williams and Eva Hunter.

"It's a huge difference in a short period of time. The result [against Australia] enhanced the desire to make change. We have lots of youth and enthusiasm," said Cunningham.

"As a squad we are probably going to be underestimated by Australia and other nations whose players predominantly play in the NRLW - and Eva [Hunter] could be one that does shock them with her physicality. She is so strong, powerful and really quick with it as well.

"Maybe that's the benefit of that scoreline in Vegas - people won't realise the talent we've got."

As in the NRL Women's Premiership (NRLW), matches at the Women's Rugby League World Cup with be played over 70 minutes, rather than 80, as it is in the Women's Super League.

Despite the improvement in standards that Women's Super League has driven, Barrow's side face an enormous task in competing with New Zealand and Australia - the only two nations to have lifted the trophy in six previous World Cups.

Players from those nations feature almost exclusively in the professional NRLW.

In contrast, the majority of the England squad have full-time jobs - as was the case four years ago.

"I know some of the girls have had to take all of their annual leave for the tournament, so they've not had a holiday all year because they've been saving it up," Leeds hooker Keara Bennett told BBC Sport.

"I think the more time we've got to invest into our training, into recovery, it just allows us to be better players and a better team.

"We're trying to create a platform and inspire the next generation, but you can't not acknowledge that money and time would really benefit and boost us."

Wigan scrum-half Isabel Rowe added: "It's definitely a struggle we have trying to make sure everybody's free and available to play.

"I don't like to use the word 'sacrifice' because we're making a choice and we choose to do it because we want to play for our country, but you have to take it into account."

England head into the wheelchair competition looking for their third title and will expect to advance from a group containing Wales, the USA and Ireland.

Head coach Tom Coyd has included five World Cup winners in his 10-player squad and the aim is simple - to replicate their triumph in 2022.

"We're going there with the attitude that we want to win," said Luis Domingos, who is one of two Sheffield Eagles players featuring.

"My goal in life is to create moments and memories, and to leave a mark. I'm confident we can win but I'm more excited about creating that memory that I can remember in 20 years.

"Me and my family - the team-mates and the staff - can create that moment, and the next generation can say: I want to do something like that."

Wales make their bow in the women's competition after progressing through qualifying but will be rank outsiders in a group containing Australia, Samoa and England, who beat them 82-0 at Headingley in 2024, and 62-0 in Neath last year.

Tom Brindle has named three players who turned out in Wales' first-ever game in 2021 against England - Leanne Burnell, Kathryn Salter and Emily Hughes.

The squad is supplemented by North Queensland Cowboys winger Sian Williams, second rower Paige Travis - who has switched allegiances from England - and Canterbury Bulldogs half-back Tayla Preston.

"My grandfather was born in Wales and grew up in Wales before moving here when he was about 20," Preston said.

"I feel really honoured to be able to play for Wales in a World Cup, and hopefully we can help grow the game for girls back in Wales and inspire them to want to play."

Most of those in the Wales ranks are taking unpaid leave to play, while the Welsh wheelchair squad raised over £10,000 via crowdfunding to help pay for costs after they lost their front-of-shirt sponsor at short notice.

Ireland and Scotland will join Wales and England at the wheelchair tournament.

While Ireland were beaten in every match in the wheelchair event four years ago, they have subsequently climbed to third in the world rankings.

And a squad containing Wigan quartet Oran Spain, Toby Burton-Carter, Mel Griffith and player-coach Phil Roberts will look to reach at least the semi-finals.

Meanwhile, Scotland face a huge challenge in a group containing France - the runners-up in 2022 - and a powerhouse Australia team who ran England close in two Tests last autumn.

But they do have a World Cup winner in their ranks. James Simpson-Hill - who helped England to victory four years ago - came out of retirement earlier this year and has switched to the nation where his father was born.

While newer rugby league nations such as Greece and Jamaica delivered a feelgood factor at the last World Cup, the men's tournament has been trimmed from 16 teams to 10 this time to reduce the number of lopsided group matches. The women's and wheelchair tournaments have both stuck with eight teams.

Familiar issues remain around the health of the game, including the levels of finance it can generate commercially and the space for an international calendar.

England's men have played just nine matches since 2022, with two of those being high-scoring and rather uncompetitive wins over France.

It is a similar same story for the Kangaroos - the sport's most successful international side - who were without a Test fixture for almost three years prior to their arrival in England in 2022 and have only had nine since.

Plans to spread the gospel of the game further by staging the tournament in the US and Canada in 2025 had to be shelved because of financial concerns and French organisers then pulled out before the International Rugby League shifted it back a year and moved it to the southern hemisphere.

With Australia's men and women the overwhelming favourites to triumph, organisers face an ongoing challenge to deliver a competitive and profitable World Cup that helps grow the game.

"I don't think the future of the game rests on this World Cup," added McDermott.

"If England win the World Cup, it'd be good. But does that mean Sky is going to treble the money that they give the clubs? The answer is no.

"And the answer would be, you know, growing the game. It's a long term [thing]. [We need to] Get in better and more sustainable investment, and there are a few more things that the game needs to do."

Sports.title: Rory McIlroy would vote to have LIV players back on PGA Tour
Sports.text:
Rory McIlroy says he would vote to have LIV Golf defectors back on the PGA Tour and believes the breakaway circuit is no longer a threat to traditional tours.

Despite securing a possible $300m (£226m) in financing from BC Partners Credit, there is ongoing uncertainty around LIV's future, with two-time major winner Jon Rahm opting out of the tour.

McIlroy, one of LIV's most fierce critics since its inception in 2022, said the circuit could have "done better things" with its vast resources, having originally been bankrolled by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund before it withdrew its backing this year.

"LIV had probably half of a good idea that was executed pretty poorly," world number two McIlroy told Bloomberg.

"They had a lot of capital but I think a lot of that capital was wasted in some ways. I think they could have used that money a lot more strategically and they could have partnered with some of the governing bodies of the game.

"They certainly could have done better things with it, instead of just enriching tour pros who were already making a lot of money."

Asked if he would vote for LIV players to return to the tours he plays on, the six-time major winner said: "Yes, I would.

"I think a rising tide lifts all boats. And I think having some of these players back is beneficial for the business of the tours, absolutely."

On Monday, the DP World Tour said players who sign up to LIV's 2027 season will not be allowed to be members of the Europe-based circuit.

McIlroy, who was speaking to Bloomberg in New Delhi before playing in the DP World India Championship, added: "It looks like every day that goes by, there's another player that was on LIV who says that they're not going to rejoin for LIV 2.0.

"So I think it is going to be very difficult for them to get out of this Chapter 11 bankruptcy and go forward.

"If they do, it's certainly not going to be a threat to the traditional order of the game as maybe it once was."

As one of the PGA Tour's biggest stars, McIlroy immediately became a vocal opponent of LIV when it fractured men's professional golf four years ago.

Asked about his long-standing criticism, he said he and 15-time major winner Tiger Woods voiced their displeasure at LIV's emergence because "we were probably the two that had the most to lose".

"We both felt this wasn't good for the game and it was going to fracture the game," he added.

"But also, everyone around the game has interests and we were about to launch TGL (Tomorrow's Golf League) and we thought LIV could have taken something away from TGL, which it did because some players went to LIV and you had to be a PGA Tour member to play in TGL.

"Everyone has different interests in the game. You're trying to protect your interests but also the interests of the game as a whole."

Sports.title: Paris St-Germain boss Luis Enrique hopes Man City will avoid sanctions
Sports.text:
Paris St-Germain boss Luis Enrique says he was surprised to learn Manchester City had been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules and hopes the club can avoid sanctions.

City host European champions PSG in the Champions League on Wednesday (20:00 BST) - their first home match since being found guilty of the majority of 115 charges.

"There is a lot of noise around Manchester City and there is often noise around big clubs," said Enrique when asked about City's guilty verdict at a news conference at Etihad Stadium on Tuesday.

"We just have to wait and see what the final decision will be. I hope everything works out well for Manchester City because I think what they have done on the pitch has been incredible over the last few years and they certainly deserved to win on the pitch all the trophies they have won.

"Now we have to wait to see what the authorities decide or the judge is going to say."

An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.

City insist they are innocent and have appealed.

Luis Enrique added: "The first thing that you hear, it is a surprise, but we need to respect the process and wait for the final decision.

"The authorities are responsible for making these decisions. But speaking only about football, they deserved those trophies. I love their football. Beyond that, we have to wait for the decision.

"The trophies you win on the pitch remain on the pitch. They deserved to win that and I hope they can avoid the sanction. But we have to wait."

Sports.title: Bournemouth open to Alex Scott sale in January
Sports.text:
Bournemouth are open to selling England midfielder Alex Scott in January under certain conditions.

The 23-year-old has been pushing to leave Vitality Stadium since rejecting two contract offers at the end of last season, but Bournemouth insisted he was not for sale throughout the recent international break.

However, after a final round of talks with his representatives, senior sources say the Cherries are willing to sanction Scott's sale if an offer of about £100m arrives in January.

Another condition will be Bournemouth's position in the Premier League table. If they are struggling towards the bottom of the league then the club may decide they need Scott to help secure survival.

It remains a significant shift in stance after a summer in which Bournemouth rejected interest from a host of clubs - with every member of the Premier League's so-called "big six" believed to have made contact to varying degrees.

All clubs were told not to make an offer or approach the player, although Chelsea tested the water with an initial £60m bid rising to £64m in add-ons which was rejected.

Chelsea and Liverpool are believed to retain an interest, with Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham having moved on to other targets over the summer.

Liverpool would be in a strong position, with manager Andoni Iraola maintaining close relationships with his former club, both with Scott himself and figures in Bournemouth's leadership.

Meanwhile, Chelsea have previously had encouragement from Scott's representatives to pursue a deal.

Scott is currently out for at least a month with a thigh injury sustained during England's 7-0 win over Croatia in the Nations League.

He remains on the same contract he signed when joining Bournemouth from Bristol City in 2023 for a fee of £25m, which expires in 2028.

The decision to consider Scott's sale is a bitter-sweet one for Bournemouth.

The club entered the season insisting none of their prized assets, including Scott, Rayan and Eli Junior Kroupi, would be sold before the summer of 2027.

However, they have since reluctantly concluded they would be prepared to let Scott leave if their valuation is met.

Bournemouth can point to a market in which spending on midfielders has reached unprecedented levels across the Premier League.

Three players have commanded fees of more than £100m in the position and the Cherries are seeking a similar amount for Scott.

A TransferRoom report, released on Tuesday, shows spending on defensive midfielders rose by "191% to 1.38bn euros , while the average fee increased by 156% to 9.9m euros - the highest average fee of any position."

There is also frustration within the club that Scott picked up an injury while away with England.

He entered the camp carrying tightness, only for the issue to worsen and leave him sidelined for about six weeks.

That came after Kroupi sustained a serious injury in pre-season, causing him to miss the entire season so far, with a return not expected until November.

New manager Marco Rose is yet to win a league match, with the 5-1 defeat by Chelsea representing the lowest point of his tenure so far.

There remains hope results will improve. Iraola endured an even longer winless run when he first took charge, while there is excitement surrounding Bournemouth's Europa League campaign.

Their European adventure began with an impressive win against Real Sociedad and continues with a home game against Sturm Graz on Thursday.

Sports.title: Billy Loughnane: Flat racing's 'Billy the Kid' set to be champion jockey at 20
Sports.text:
Billy Loughnane had never ridden in a professional race this time four years ago.

Now he is set to be crowned Flat racing's champion jockey.

And, at just 20, he's the youngest person to do so in more than a century - which means he hasn't yet shaken off the nickname "Billy the Kid".

"It's been an extraordinary couple of years, really," said Loughnane.

"I didn't think it would snowball into what it's become."

In January 2023, BBC Sport went to visit Loughnane at his family's racing yard in Worcestershire.

As a 16-year-old, he was taking the racing world by storm, racking up more than 20 winners in the first few weeks of the year - temporarily putting him top of the flat jockey standings.

He insisted then that people needed to "calm down".

While being champion apprentice was his goal, becoming the champion jockey was a dream that felt a "long way off".

Yet, remarkably, here we are.

This Saturday, on Champions Day at Ascot, Loughnane will lift the trophy.

When asked what he would have thought if someone had told him that when he drove up to Newcastle for his first race as an apprentice jockey in October 2022, he said: "I'd have said, 'that's absolutely crazy, what have you been drinking?'"

Despite being in a strong position to take the title, Loughnane admitted he felt the pressure "not to let it slip" until a few weeks ago.

But his nearest challenger Oisin Murphy waved the white flag, knowing he couldn't catch him, and that's when he started to enjoy it.

The final winning margin is likely to be significant - Loughnane currently leads Murphy by 29 with 222 winners.

Yet he is not stopping there.

The young star wants to break Sir Gordon Richards' 1947 record on the Flat of 269 winners in a calendar year.

"Yeah, it's in my sights," added the Irishman, who is the son of trainer Mark Loughnane.

"I'm just going to take the rest of this month in November and then assess in December if I feel it's possible, realistically. But it is in my sights, something that I'm looking towards. I'm not blinkers on full blasting at the moment, but I'm just going to keep riding every day as much as possible and assess the situation."

He could also reach his idol Sir AP McCoy's record of 289 winners, which was set over jumps as he said: "I'll be giving it my best shot until the start of December."

Loughnane's partnership with trainer George Boughey has been pivotal to his career, and the pair have enjoyed considerable success this year.

He rode the Boughey-trained Bow Echo to three Grade 1 victories, the highlight being the 2,000 Guineas at Newmarket.

"I've been searching for that feeling again," added Loughnane.

"I mean, the reception after Goodwood [winning the Sussex Stakes, also on Bow Echo] was pretty electric as well to be fair and I'm glad that I did showcase him after the race at Goodwood because obviously it was his final run. But the best buzz of winning a race was the 2,000 [Guineas]."

While jockeys are known to keep notes, few if any are perhaps quite as meticulous as Loughnane, who has a Whatsapp group just with himself, where he compiles notes on every horse he rides.

Does he think it sets him apart?

"Maybe not sets me apart, but I do think it is an advantage to be able to help," he said. "I sit on a lot of horses in the year. I've sat on over 1,000 already this year, and it's hard to keep track of absolutely every one. I wouldn't be doing my job properly if I wasn't."

So after racing on Saturday is finished and he has the trophy, what could the celebrations look like?

He admits he doesn't really know.

It's a sign of his age - and how busy he's been focused on the championship - that he has not been involved in the planning.

"My mother's actually sorted it out, so I actually don't have a clue where I'm going," added Loughnane.

"But it's with my family, friends, girlfriend, and all the sponsors and people that have helped me, sort of since I've had ponies, the whole way up, will be there.

"So there'll be a big group of us and it's more of a celebration than anything else.

"But as to what I'm eating, I'm not actually sure."

Sports.title: Atlético Madrid v Manchester United: Champions League – live
Sports.text:
When last they met. Ralf Rangnick, there’s a blast from the recent past, but a forgotten name already.

Peadar de Burca gets in touch: “This is one of those games, John, where you don’t tune it to see free-flowing joga bonita, dancing on the ceiling football, but because there’s a whiff in the air, a whiff of wounded sheep, the wolves are closing in and by cuss it’s hard to pull your eyes away. The beginning of the end for Carrick...?”

In August, in a friendly in Sweden, United and Atletico played a friendly, United winning 2-1. Who came on in the 82nd minute? None other than JJ Gabriel? Whatever happened to him?

Josh Keeling also has his theories: “I reckon it might be a diamond with Fernandes behind a front two. Or maybe Fernandes as a false nine. Let’s see.”

Whisper it, but Bruno has not been playing well this season. He did not complete a pass for a long time against Tottenham, and there’s been that hint from the international break that he’s been playing with an injury.

Sean McHale gets in touch: “Looks like Bruno at false nine, John. I think a good shout as they’ve been far too open in a de facto 4-4-2. And Tielemans not great in a two.”

Carrick said that we would have to “wait and see” when asked about Bruno, so that suggests Sean may be right there.

Diego Simeone made mention of Julian Alvarez in his pre-match duties: “Well, he’s happy because I’ve been able to speak to him a lot and I’ve really focussed on Julian Alvarez as the person, not just the player and I think we’ve reached reached a very good point with him.“

Michael Carrick speaks to the Amazon UK broadcast: “It’s where we want to be. Got a really good history of this competition and that’s where we want to challenge ourselves and test ourselves. you know, we’ve worked hard to be here. We want a reaction You know, we haven’t had the results that we wanted, that we expected. Fine margins in some of them games and it can go both ways, but the reality is exactly where we are now and this is a fresh opportunity.

“I think we want a get control without the ball and we want a lot more control with it whatever get. I think we’ve got a bit of flexibility. I think we need to defend as a whole team. But you have proved that we’re capable of doing that and we got to get back to that.”

For Atleti, Koke missing, as mentioned previously, but Julian Alvarez, who wanted to leave the club in the summer, is a starter. His last start was against Liverpool, so this is his first home start of the season.

That United team looks like Youri Tielemans is being pushed forward and Bruno Fernandes will be playing off the flanks. Marcus Rashford returns to the starting lineup. Baleba added some energy to United on Saturday against Tottenham though his shooting was a little wayward. Is that Dalot or Yoro at left-back? Would guess Yoro. Andrey Santos for the double pivot, too.

Updated at 13.58 EDT

Teams: Baleba starts for United

Atlético Madrid: Oblak, Llorente, Romero, Hancko, Grimaldo, Simeone, Barrios, Cardoso, Alex Baena, Alvarez, Lee. Subs: Musso, Mendoza, Sorloth, Lookmnan, David, Ortiz, Pubill, Hjulmand, Le Normand, Lituba, Dani Martinez, Castillo.

Manchester United: Lammens, Dalot, Martinez, Heaven, Yoro, Santos, Baleba, Tielemans, B.Fernandes, Rashford, Mbeumo. Subs: Darlow, Mee, Amass, Armer, De Ligt, Maguire, Mount, T.Fletcher, Lacey, Amad, Cunha, Zirkzee.

Michael Carrick was not exactly bullish – he never is – but he remains publicly calm under pressure.

double quotation markWe hoped for a lot more, we expected a lot more, and we are where we are. I was aware that, winning as many as we had [last season], it was going to get more challenging, stickier. I understand that when it is not going well there is a real clamour and a feeling that it’s a disaster, that it’s all wrong and that everything needs to be changed. I kind of get that, but that’s not our mindset and it’s certainly not mine. You have to deal with things and overcome them. That is what I did throughout my career. We have to accept reality but we are building and you can’t lose sight of the journey.

It feels a long time since Manchester United played Sabah on their opening group-stage match.

There will be 3,750 United fans in the stands. They have not had much to cheer this season.

Atlético Madrid captain Koke will not play tonight after his mother died.

There will be a moment of silence before the game at the Metropolitano Stadium, and the home team’s players will wear black armbands. Koke’s brother, Borja Resurrección, is an assistant coach of Atletico’s under-19 squad. The club’s flag outside the Metropolitano is flying at half-mast

With Manchester United and Michael Carrick careering towards the dumper, then travelling to face Diego Simeone’s Atleti is almost certainly not the fixture that would be handpicked. Though perhaps it can serve as some kind of turning point. Play as sluggishly as United have in their last two Premier League matches either side of the international break – Fulham and Tottenham – and there’s big trouble in store. Atlético have won their last four matches in La Liga, including a famous win in the Madrid derby. Their last Champions League match did, thouugh, see them lose at Anfield. If the competition’s bloated structure has its critics, and United can probably get away with losing in the scheme of reaching the knockouts, Carrick can barely afford to. Further to that, there may not be two more opposite touchline characters than Simeone and Carrick.

Kick-off is at 8pm UK time. Join me.
